title: V Engineering develops new hybrid battery for McLaren P1 - Automotive Testing Technology International
content: V Engineering, McLaren’s independent engineering center, has announced that it is developing a new high-voltage, hybrid battery solution for the McLaren P1, as part of Project Continuum. The original hybrid battery cells used in the P1 were manufactured in 2010. After 16 years of service, numerous units have deteriorated to the point that they must be replaced, otherwise the car will be undriveable. Project Continuum from V Engineering offers current and future McLaren P1 owners an alternative high-voltage battery solution that improves energy storage and reduces the overall weight of the original battery with no penalty to the existing power delivery. Another key user feature of the new battery is that it offers extended EV range compared with the factory production unit. Developed in collaboration with engineers involved in the original P1 program, the battery features a glycol-based cooling system with significantly improved heat rejection properties from the newly developed cells. The battery solution is built around a proven, high-performance 21700 lithium battery module engineered to FIA Formula E requirements to offer motorsport-grade technology. The plug-and-play approach from V Engineering reportedly improves performance and reliability while retaining compatibility with the vehicle’s existing electrical architecture. Along with the advanced cooling properties of the new battery, design also focused on the energy storage capacity of the new unit, which has been increased to 12.4kWh compared with the standard 4.72kWh of the original P1. Customer installations are scheduled to begin in spring 2027, with V Engineering currently in discussions with owners from the UK and Europe, the Middle East and the USA. Project Continuum is the first phase of a broader powertrain development program intended to provide long-term technical support for McLaren P1 owners. title: V of BTS helps Champion reset for a new generation - Fashion United
content: Champion is turning to K-Pop star V of BTS to help reposition the century-old athletic brand for a new generation of consumers. The company has named V, also known as Kim Taehyung, the face of its new “True Champion” campaign, a global initiative that spotlights athletes, artists and creators whose influence is defined as much by individuality and cultural impact as by performance. Announced on Monday, the partnership marks what Champion calls “a new chapter” for the brand. The True Champion campaign is designed to celebrate people “shaping today’s culture through their originality, perspective and enduring impact,” bringing together figures from sport, music and the broader creative community. Stefani Fleurant, EVP, marketing, sport and lifestyle at Authentic, cited V’s “creative vision, global influence and genuine connection with his audience” as the reasons he is a “natural partner” for the brand. V’s appointment comes as brands across fashion and lifestyle increasingly use K-Pop ambassadors to drive awareness and sales among Gen Z and millennial audiences. The list includes high luxury brands such as Dior, Louis Vuitton, Chanel and more. Champion described V as “known for his unmistakable style, artistic vision and global reach,” and noted that his influence “extends beyond music, leaving an indelible mark across fashion, art and popular culture while connecting with millions of fans worldwide.” The campaign’s wider cast reinforces that strategy. Joining V in the fall/winter 2026 True Champion campaign are Romeo Beckham, musical duo Sofi Tukker, NBA player Kyle Kuzma, singer and actor Danna Paola, hockey player Megan Keller, swimmer Bella Sims and creator Jaalen Best.  Together, the group is presented as a diverse cross-section of Champion’s global community, illustrating how the brand is broadening its definition of what it means to be a “champion” today beyond traditional sports.

title: Champion Names BTS’ V the Face of Its Global “True Champion” Campaign - stupidDOPE
content: Few apparel brands possess the kind of cultural history that Champion carries into 2026. Its script logo and familiar “C” have moved through college athletics, professional sports, hip-hop, skateboarding, streetwear, luxury collaborations, and everyday wardrobes without becoming permanently confined to any one of those worlds. That adaptability has always been central to Champion’s relevance. The brand’s latest global campaign appears designed to make that quality explicit. Champion has named V of BTS as the face of “True Champion,” a new worldwide campaign launching with the brand’s Fall/Winter 2026 season. The South Korean singer-songwriter leads a deliberately multidisciplinary cast that includes Romeo Beckham, SOFI TUKKER, NBA player Kyle Kuzma, Mexican singer and actor Danna Paola, ice hockey player Megan Keller, Olympic swimmer Bella Sims, and actor Jaalen Best. The casting is broad by design. Rather than defining a champion exclusively through athletic accomplishment, Champion is using the campaign to recognize people working across music, sports, entertainment, and contemporary culture. V becomes a particularly significant figure within that strategy because his influence crosses several of those categories at once. For a company whose identity has repeatedly traveled beyond its original athletic context, the message feels appropriately aligned with its history. “True Champion” is ultimately less about abandoning sports than acknowledging what the language of sportswear has become: a global cultural vocabulary shaped by athletes, artists, musicians, designers, and audiences who rarely remain within clearly defined categories. Selecting V as the campaign’s central figure immediately establishes the international scale Champion intends for “True Champion.” As a member of BTS and an established solo artist, V has developed an audience that extends far beyond conventional pop fandom. His cultural visibility encompasses music, fashion, photography, art, and luxury, creating an unusually broad platform from which Champion can communicate its next chapter. Celebrity partnerships have become so common within fashion that name recognition alone rarely guarantees meaningful impact. The more effective relationships emerge when the individual contributes a recognizable point of view that complements the brand rather than simply appearing beside its products. His public image has consistently incorporated an appreciation for fashion that moves between contemporary luxury, tailoring, vintage references, relaxed casualwear, and carefully considered styling. That versatility gives Champion considerable room to operate. The partnership does not require V to become an athlete or Champion to become a luxury house. Both can meet within the increasingly expansive territory occupied by modern sportswear. The relationship also reflects the changing geography of cultural influence. American heritage brands now operate within a marketplace where music, style, entertainment, and consumer behavior are shaped simultaneously across Seoul, London, Los Angeles, Mexico City, Paris, New York, and countless other cultural centers. Choosing a BTS member as the campaign’s leading face acknowledges that reality directly. Champion’s campaign premise is notable because it loosens the traditional definition of its own name. Historically, the word “champion” carries an obvious competitive meaning. It belongs naturally to sports, tournaments, records, trophies, and measurable achievement. For an athletic brand, that association requires little explanation. By assembling athletes alongside musicians, actors, and other cultural figures, Champion positions individuality and creative conviction as achievements worthy of the same language. The company describes the campaign around people who redefine boundaries through originality and distinctive perspectives, effectively moving championship status away from the scoreboard. The approach reflects a broader transformation within sportswear. Athletic brands once relied heavily on performance credentials to establish cultural authority. Contemporary audiences engage with them differently. Performance still matters, but music, design, fashion, entertainment, and personal expression have become equally important channels through which sportswear acquires meaning. Champion has historical credibility within this intersection because its clothing migrated into popular culture organically long before cross-disciplinary collaborations became standard marketing practice. “True Champion” gives that history a contemporary framework. Champion’s relevance cannot be understood entirely through advertising campaigns or celebrity endorsements. Much of its cultural significance comes from the garments themselves. The company’s relationship with the sweatshirt is particularly important. Champion helped develop apparel that became foundational to American athletic clothing, including innovations associated with durable fleece construction and the Reverse Weave technique. What began as practical sportswear eventually became part of the broader uniform of American casual dress. That journey is important because it explains why Champion can credibly place musicians beside professional athletes today. Sweatshirts and hoodies stopped belonging exclusively to locker rooms decades ago. They became campus clothing, workwear, streetwear, skate apparel, hip-hop staples, fashion pieces, and everyday essentials. Champion traveled with them through each transition. The brand consequently occupies an unusual position. It can reference genuine athletic heritage without appearing dependent upon performance culture alone. That flexibility becomes particularly valuable in 2026, when consumers increasingly resist rigid distinctions between athletic clothing, streetwear, luxury, and casual apparel. The wider “True Champion” cast reinforces the campaign’s central idea through contrast. Romeo Beckham brings a connection to soccer and fashion culture. Kyle Kuzma occupies the increasingly visible intersection between professional basketball and personal style. Megan Keller and Bella Sims represent elite athletic performance through hockey and swimming, respectively. SOFI TUKKER, Danna Paola, and Jaalen Best broaden the campaign through music and acting. Placed alongside V, these figures create something closer to a cultural cross-section than a conventional endorsement roster. That structure reflects the way contemporary audiences actually consume culture. A person following the NBA may simultaneously care about Korean pop, European football, streetwear, electronic music, film, and fashion. Digital platforms have collapsed many of the boundaries that once separated those interests, allowing cultural identities to become more layered and geographically diverse. The most relevant global campaigns increasingly avoid speaking to a single archetypal consumer. They construct networks of personalities capable of entering different communities while remaining connected through a central idea. Champion’s selection of talent suggests an understanding of that fragmented environment. Kyle Kuzma’s inclusion carries particular resonance for a brand rooted in American sports. Professional basketball has become one of fashion’s most productive cultural environments. The NBA tunnel functions as an unofficial runway, athletes collaborate directly with designers, and players increasingly establish identities that extend well beyond performance. Kuzma has participated prominently in that evolution. His approach to clothing has frequently challenged conventional expectations surrounding athlete style, making experimentation part of his broader public persona. Within “True Champion,” that willingness to treat fashion as personal expression aligns naturally with the campaign’s emphasis on individuality. His presence also creates continuity between Champion’s athletic foundations and the campaign’s expanded cultural ambitions. The message is not that sports have become less important. Instead, athletes themselves now operate across broader cultural territories. The campaign arrives at a moment when sportswear has become difficult to separate from everyday fashion. Sweatshirts, athletic shorts, jerseys, sneakers, track jackets, caps, and performance-inspired garments are no longer secondary components of wardrobes. They are foundational pieces worn across work, travel, leisure, entertainment, and social environments. That ubiquity has changed what consumers expect from heritage athletic brands. History remains valuable, but heritage alone cannot sustain relevance. Brands must demonstrate an ability to interpret their archives through contemporary culture without reducing decades of identity to nostalgia. Its recognizable branding, collegiate associations, athletic heritage, and longstanding relationship with street culture provide a foundation newer labels cannot manufacture quickly. The challenge lies in presenting those assets to younger global audiences who may encounter Champion through music or fashion before learning about its sporting history. BTS has played a significant role in demonstrating how contemporary musicians can influence global fashion without being restricted to a single aesthetic. The group’s members have developed distinct identities, creating individual relationships with fashion while maintaining the enormous cultural visibility associated with BTS collectively. That distinction has become increasingly important as each member’s creative output has expanded. V’s particular appeal comes partly from an image that resists easy categorization. There is an appreciation for classic clothing and vintage references alongside contemporary designer fashion. Formalwear can coexist with relaxed silhouettes. Highly styled appearances sit comfortably beside more understated moments. For Champion, that range is useful because it reinforces the versatility inherent in sportswear itself. A sweatshirt can be deeply ordinary and culturally significant at the same time. Its meaning changes according to the person wearing it, the context surrounding it, and the styling choices made around it. V’s participation allows Champion to communicate that flexibility to an enormous international audience without requiring the clothing to become something fundamentally different. Champion’s contemporary challenge extends beyond competing against other sportswear companies. Modern consumers navigate a marketplace filled with heritage athletic brands, independent streetwear labels, luxury houses, direct-to-consumer companies, vintage clothing, resale platforms, and rapidly emerging designers. Attention is fragmented, and cultural relevance can shift quickly. Within that environment, established history provides an advantage only when it remains active. Campaigns such as “True Champion” allow Champion to reconnect its heritage with the present rather than treating its archive as a museum piece. The strategy recognizes that authenticity is not simply a matter of age. It comes from understanding what made a brand culturally useful in the first place and finding contemporary expressions of the same underlying values. Champion’s strongest historical asset may be precisely this adaptability. Its clothing has repeatedly been adopted by communities beyond those for which it was initially designed. The significance of “True Champion” will ultimately depend on what follows the campaign. Celebrity casting can generate attention, but sustained cultural relevance requires product, storytelling, distribution, and design to support the message. Champion possesses the historical foundation necessary to make that possible, while the Fall/Winter 2026 campaign gives the company a highly visible international platform from which to articulate its direction. V serves as an especially effective centerpiece because his career represents the kind of boundary-crossing identity the campaign celebrates. Music remains central, but fashion, visual culture, art, and global influence exist alongside it. The broader cast extends that idea across athletics and entertainment without requiring every participant to represent the same form of achievement. That may be the campaign’s most relevant observation. Sportswear has spent decades moving beyond sports while never entirely leaving them behind. Champion helped shape that transition through products that became cultural staples precisely because people found uses for them beyond their original purpose. “True Champion” brings that history into the present by recognizing that contemporary influence rarely belongs to a single discipline. It develops wherever talent, individuality, and cultural perspective intersect. Champion’s Fall/Winter 2026 “True Champion” campaign featuring BTS’ V is launching globally alongside Romeo Beckham, SOFI TUKKER, Kyle Kuzma, Danna Paola, Megan Keller, Bella Sims, and Jaalen Best. title: Sharks v All Blacks prediction: Springbok-shorn hosts to 'make a memory' in Greatest Rivalry clash - Planet Rugby
content:
Could Ma'a Nonu face off with Jordie Barrett in the Sharks v All Blacks clash? The All Blacks arrive in Durban with a side carrying much of Dave Rennie’s Test spine, a scrum that was pulled apart in Cape Town and rain forecast for the full 80 minutes. The Sharks arrive without eight Springboks, without a senior fixture since their URC season ended in May, and with a 44-year-old All Black on the bench as Kings Park hosts another warm-up to an historic series ahead. The top line is that Kings Park has been waiting 34 years for this, and the team that turns up to mark the occasion is somewhere between 70 and 80 per cent of itself. Natal last played New Zealand in 1992, a 43-25 defeat that is still spoken of in Durban as one of the great club-versus-country nights. No side wearing the Sharks name has ever faced the All Blacks and the 1996 tourists, whose series win is being commemorated across this whole eight-match schedule, never came to Durban for a provincial fixture at all. So the ledger reads six matches against Natal, five New Zealand wins and the 6-6 draw of 1960 that remains the province’s high-water mark against them. JP Pietersen has been honest about the state of his squad, which is the correct call when the alternative is pretending. Bongi Mbonambi, Trevor Nyakane, Jason Jenkins and both Hendrikse brothers are injured. Aphelele Fassi, Ethan Hooker, Eben Etzebeth and André Esterhuizen are with the Springboks. Emile van Heerden pulled out on Monday, and Vincent Tshituka failed a head injury assessment, which cost the Sharks a starting lock and a replacement forward inside 24 hours. What is left is six players from the South Africa A side that beat Zimbabwe 40-0 in June, a 62-cap Test tighthead, a flanker reaching a century for the union, and a senior side whose URC season finished on May 16. Rennie, meanwhile, has stopped experimenting. Seven of the side that beat the Stormers 38-21 are retained in the 23, but the rest of this team is close to the one that will start at Ellis Park on August 22. Damian McKenzie, Jordie Barrett, Quinn Tupaea, Ruben Love, Tupou Vaa’i, Luke Jacobson, Wallace Sititi, Fletcher Newell and Ethan de Groot were all held back in Cape Town. They are here now, which tells you Rennie did not like what he watched on Friday. He is also comfortable enough with the fixture to hand Bradley Slater and Semisi Ta’eiloa first appearances off the bench. Start at the scrum, because that is where the Stormers found the tour’s first crack and Vincent Koch will have watched every replay with popcorn in hand and domination in mind. New Zealand conceded 16 penalties in Cape Town and took three yellow cards, two of them inside 90 seconds in the 11th and 12th minutes, at one point playing with 13 men. Pasilio Tosi was penalised four times in 47 minutes, and several of those came at scrum time. The reserves did not repair it. Rennie has responded by starting De Groot and Newell, a considerable upgrade, but Koch has 63 Tests behind him and a specific brief. If the Sharks can win two or three scrum penalties in the opening quarter, they get the only currency available to them tonight, which is territory, and they get referee Matt Carley thinking about a pattern. All Blacks latest: Dave Rennie forced into late reshuffle as key man withdraws from Sharks showdown Then look up. The Stormers put Beauden Barrett under a sustained aerial assault through Yaqeen Ahmed and Dewaldt Duvenage and the All Blacks did not deal with it, a point Rennie conceded without much attempt at spin. Now it rains in Durban and Bradley Davids and Vusi Moyo will kick early and often because it’s the quickest route to success for a side this short of running firepower, and McKenzie, Caleb Clarke and a one-cap Fehi Fineanganofo form a back three that is quick and dangerous rather than tall and settled. Wet ball, a young Sharks chase and a New Zealand aerial system that has already been found out once is the single most plausible route to an upset, or at least to a scoreline that stays respectable past the hour. The personnel have changed almost entirely since Friday. The question is whether the structure has. The third question is conditioning, and it works entirely against the hosts. The Stormers were level at 14-14 until the 66th minute and then lost the game in 10 minutes as three tries went past them. The Sharks are in pre-season and their senior season ended in May. Whatever their intent, the last quarter is where a 44-man touring squad with a bench loaded with fresh international forwards does its work, and Ollie Norris, Tosi and Ethan Blackadder arriving against tiring legs is not a fair fight. Pietersen has framed the evening as an occasion rather than a contest, which is both realistic and rather good management. He told his players to “make a memory” they would still be discussing in 30 years, and said facing the haka in Durban would be a wonderful experience for a young group. On the state of his team, he was blunt: the Sharks will not be at 100 per cent, at best 70 or 80, and they will give it everything they have. He also confirmed the Sharks will pass on whatever they learn to the Springboks, which is the honest admission that this fixture has a purpose beyond itself. On selecting Ma’a Nonu, brought to Durban last Tuesday to mentor the outside backs and named in the reserves seven days later, Pietersen was unapologetic. “His name says it all,” he said, before pointing out that the man supposedly displaced, Jurenzo Julius, is in fact starting at 13. Ex-England winger claims All Blacks star has Cheslin Kolbe for speed but footwork is ‘best there’s ever been’ Rennie’s tone has been the opposite: less occasion, more repair work. He described Cape Town as an introduction to South African rugby and a proud province, admitted his side gave away too many scrum penalties and never solved the aerial contest, and said flatly that they will be better. On handing Luke Jacobson the captaincy for the first time, he called him the obvious choice, respected in the group and a leader through actions rather than words. 20-year-old Vusi Moyo became the youngest fly-half ever capped by South Africa last month against Wales. Rain, a retreating pack for long stretches and Love opposite him is a considerable evening’s work, and how he handles the kicking duel will decide whether the Sharks have any platform at all. Meanwhile, Phepsi Buthelezi makes his 100th appearance for the Sharks, at blindside, against the All Blacks, in Durban. There are worse ways to reach a century, and he is the closest thing this pack has to a senior organising voice. For New Zealand, Wallace Sititi is back in the number eight shirt with a Test place to secure inside 10 days. In a game New Zealand should control, the way he carries in the wet is the sort of evidence Rennie is actually collecting here. In the backline, Kyle Preston has only had 242 minutes of rugby all season after a full Crusaders campaign spent on the bench. He gets a first start at scrum-half with Cortez Ratima behind him and Cam Roigard rested as a precaution. He is auditioning for the right to be Roigard’s understudy in a four-Test series. Last but by no means least, Ma’a Nonu. Two World Cups, 103 caps, and a Sharks debut off the bench against his own country at 44. Sentiment aside, he still knows precisely where the space is. This is the contest with genuine consequences beyond tonight. Vincent Koch is the last serious Test forward standing in a depleted Sharks pack, a scrummager with 63 caps who spent years plying his trade in the Premiership and who now gets a direct look at the loosehead Rennie intends to start at Ellis Park. Ethan de Groot was rested in Cape Town precisely so he could be fresh for this, and he arrives knowing that his replacements were comprehensively beaten by a Stormers front-row that was not even at full strength. Sir Steve Hansen’s bold ‘100 per cent’ Richie Mo’unga claim as ex-All Blacks boss backs Dave Rennie to make ‘right decision’ Everything the Springboks want to do to New Zealand on August 22 runs through this scrummaging question, and Rassie Erasmus will have a coach on the phone tomorrow morning asking Koch exactly what he felt. If De Groot holds and the New Zealand eight starts marching, the Cape Town evidence looks like a second-string aberration. If Koch gets underneath him and Carley starts reaching for his arm, a four-Test series acquires a theme before it has begun. And one for the purist, if the timing falls right. Nonu is on the bench at 23 and Jordie Barrett starts at 12. Should the pair share the field for even 10 minutes, Kings Park gets a collision between the man who defined the modern All Blacks midfield and the man who inherited the job. Nonu won his first cap in 2003, when Barrett was six years old, and he arrives at 44 with two World Cup medals and no obvious reason to be doing this beyond wanting to. It will not decide the match. It is the reason a certain sort of supporter will stay in their seat for the last quarter. The Sharks will be excellent for half an hour. Kings Park in the rain, the first Haka before a Durban provincial side since 1992, a pack with nothing to lose and a referee likely to reward the side going forward at scrum time should give them a foothold, and a young backline with Nonu’s fingerprints on its preparation will not be short of belief. Then the bench arrives, the legs go, and the difference between something approaching a Test side and a provincial side in pre-season becomes arithmetic. New Zealand will be tidier than they were in Cape Town without being anything like the finished article, which is the point of the exercise. The rain keeps the score down and the Sharks get the memory Pietersen asked for. Want more from Planet Rugby? BTS’ V is no stranger to the spotlight, and when it comes to becoming the face of a major brand, the K-pop superstar seems to be a natural fit. title: Hybrid SUV faceoff: Comparing the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V - usatoday.com
content: What is the RAV4's infotainment screen size compared to the CR-V Hybrid? How does the Jeep Cherokee's fuel economy compare to the RAV4 and CR-V? Why is the RAV4 more affordable than the CR-V Hybrid? Following Toyota’s decision to discontinue the gas RAV4 powertrain, the 2026 Toyota RAV4 will only be offered as a standard small hybrid SUV. One of its fiercest rivals in the 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid. Both Japanese automakers produce practical family SUVs that deliver solid gas mileage thanks to electric motors. Here's how the RAV4 and CR-V Hybrid compare when it comes to pricing, specs standard features and more. The 2026 Toyota RAV4 is a completely redesigned compact SUV ushering in the nameplate's sixth generation. It introduces a new exterior styling, interior design and standard powertrain. Toyota's small hybrid SUV starts at $31,900. It uses a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine and electric motors to produce 226 horsepower. The RAV4 achieves 47 miles per gallon in the city and 40 miles per gallon on the highway. It has stellar fuel economy for its segment and 37.8 cubic feet of cargo space. Toyota's small hybrid SUV is affordable, spacious enough for small families and has a long history of reliability. Honda still offers a gas version of its CR-V small SUV, but its hybrid iteration gets better gas mileage and delivers the same driving verve and handling that fans have come to love. Honda's CR-V Hybrid is pricier than Toyota's model, but it provides more value to driving enthusiasts. The 2026 Honda CR-V Hybrid starts at $35,630. It uses a 2.0-liter four-cylinder engine and electric motors to produce 204 horsepower. The small hybrid SUV achieves 43 miles per gallon in the city and 36 miles per gallon on the highway. I tested the 2026 CR-V Hybrid and found it fun to drive. It has 39.3 cubic feet of cargo space, making its cargo area even roomier than the RAV4's. The CR-V feels refined for a mainstream family SUV and is well-balanced. The greatest noticeable difference between the two Japanese small hybrid SUVs is their respective starting prices. Opting for the CR-V Hybrid over the RAV4 will run you an additional $3,730 before taxes and fees. That price difference gets you a slightly classier family SUV with a bit more cargo space. Toyota's RAV4 comes standard with a 10.5 inch infotainment system screen, which is 1.5 inches longer than the CR-V Hybrid's standard screen. When it comes to value for the money, the Toyota RAV4 s tough to beat because it's significantly more affordable and boasts superior gas mileage. In terms of quality and handling, the CR-V Hybrid has the upper hand. Drivers who find the RAV4 base model too barebones can upgrade to the SE trim for $34,700 and get upgrades like heated front seats and a smart key system. If you can look past the RAV4's interior quality, it's the better small hybrid SUV for the money for drivers in search of value. If you're a driving enthusiast and want a smooth ride and premium materials, the CR-V Hybrid is worth the price difference between the two models. title: Stellar Cartography: SDSS-V Releases Latest All-sky Spectra Including First Optical Spectra From The Southern Hemisphere - Astrobiology Web
content:
[Carnegie Institution for Science]   The Sloan Digital Sky Survey V (SDSS-V) has announced its twentieth public data release (DR20), delivering a dramatic expansion of the Milky Way Mapper (MWM) scientific survey—the most detailed spectroscopic map yet assembled of stars in and around our home galaxy. With repeat visits, DR20 includes more than two million total spectra, revealing the temperatures, ages, and chemical compositions of stars all across the Milky Way. The dataset draws on observations from twin optical spectrographs at Apache Point Observatory in New Mexico and Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, giving astronomers a seamless view of stellar populations across both the northern and southern skies. “It’s exciting to release such a massive catalog of high-quality spectra to the public,” said Dr. Marina Kounkel, assistant professor at University of North Florida and SDSS-V Survey Coordinator. She continued, “These data have already been extensively used by SDSS collaboration to enable a wide variety of scientific studies, but this is all just scratching the surface of what these data make possible.” Among the release’s centerpiece results is the first major public dataset from the MWM Halo Program, which maps the faint, sparse stellar shroud enveloping the Milky Way’s disk. These ancient stars preserve a fossil record of the galaxy’s formation and its history of engulfing smaller satellite galaxies. Across three complementary frontiers, the Halo program presents spectra of 250,000 halo stars including a full-sky survey of giant stars reaching more than 65,000 light-years away, fast-moving stars within 3,000 light-years of Earth, and pristine cosmic relics. This targeted hunt for ultra-metal-poor stars with iron levels less than 1% of the Sun, has already yielded the most pristine star in the Universe discovered by a class of undergrads at the University of Chicago. “We’ve had a wonderful time exploring this dataset,” said Deputy Project Scientist Alexander Ji of the University of Chicago. He continued “we can’t wait to see what everyone else will do with it.” Mapping out the metal-poor outer halo of the Milky Way provides an important connection to the early Universe. Their chemical signatures and their orbital dynamics within the halo provide important clues for galaxy formation and evolution. A recent study led by Harvard graduate student Vedant Chandra is using SDSS-V data to map out these objects. “The Milky Way’s distant halo contains the fossil record of our Galaxy’s formation, but reading that record requires a truly all-sky view” said Vedant Chandra. “With SDSS-V, we can measure the motions, distances, and chemical compositions of halo stars across both hemispheres—allowing us to discover ancient stellar structures and map the dynamics of the Galaxy on an unprecedented scale. DR20 places this uniquely powerful dataset in the hands of the worldwide astronomical community.” Data Release 20 more than doubles the number of white dwarf stars available to the public from SDSS, adding 49,000 white dwarf spectra. White dwarfs are the dense, cooling remnants left behind when stars the size of our Sun exhaust their nuclear fuel. Over 80 percent of these white dwarfs had never been observed by SDSS before and over 40 percent lie in the southern sky—filling a critical observational gap in a region historically underserved by major spectroscopic surveys. These spectra preserve a direct record of how stars die, while their atmospheres frequently reveal telltale chemical signatures of shredded planetary bodies that once orbited them. “This data release offers tens of thousands of new spectra of dead stars, many of which bear the signatures of remnant planetary systems that survived the evolution of their host star,” said Prof. JJ Hermes, a Milky Way Mapper Survey Scientist based at Boston University. “To collect this many spectra of white dwarfs, one by one, would have taken decades.” A Complete Neighborhood Watch Within 300 Light-Years Closer to home, the Solar Neighborhood Census is building the most complete spectroscopic map to date of objects within 250 parsecs of the Sun. This study releases spectra for 280,000 nearby stellar neighbors, focusing on low-mass M dwarfs and brown dwarfs that make up three out of every four stars in our galaxy. By pairing SDSS-V spectroscopy with precise distances from the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Gaia satellite, astronomers now have a new benchmark dataset for understanding how stellar mass, age, and composition vary in our cosmic backyard. The expanded Young Galaxy Program quadrupled in scale from DR19 to DR20 and now encompasses over 200,000 young stars and planetary nurseries. Young stars still surrounded by planet-forming disks of gas and dust, displaying intense magnetic activity, are sun-like infants. The study also locates massive OB stars, whose recent formation outline the Milky Way’s spiral arms. In an ongoing collaboration with ESA’s eROSITA X-ray space telescope, SDSS-V has gathered nearly 48,000 optical spectra of targets identified as energetic X-ray sources. This dataset matches high-energy space signals with their physical host stars—including accreting binary systems and magnetic stars—creating the largest joint optical/X-ray catalog assembled to date. “Every stellar spectrum tells a story, and DR20 marks another step towards building a lasting spectroscopic legacy of our Galaxy,” said Dr. Andrew Tkachenko, from KU Leuven, Program Head for the Milky Way Mapper . “By making high-quality optical spectra of millions of stars publicly available, the SDSS-V Milky Way Mapper is enabling discoveries that will deepen our understanding of the Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds, and the life cycles of stars.” Parallel to Data Release 20, a new study led by Lucey et al. (2026, ApJL, Vol. 1000, L44) utilizes SDSS-V data to announce the discovery of the first five carbon-enhanced metal-poor (CEMP) stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC). This extends the study of these ancient stellar fossils beyond the Milky Way for the first time, offering crucial clues about how the universe’s earliest supernovae seeded neighboring galaxies with chemical elements. “Carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars give us a rare window into the oldest stars in the universe, ones that formed when the cosmos had far less heavy elements (like iron and oxygen) than it does today.” said Dr. Maddie Lucey. One of the biggest open questions about these stars is how much their nature depends on the galaxy they formed in. Do we expect the oldest stars in the Milky Way to be different from the oldest stars in a galaxy roughly a tenth its size, like the LMC? While tens of thousands of carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars have been discovered in the Milky Way, searches in the LMC, limited by smaller samples of stars, had previously come up empty, suggesting fundamental differences between the oldest stars in these two galaxies. Dr. Lucey continued, “the large SDSS-V sample enabled us to discover the first five carbon-enhanced metal-poor stars in the LMC, providing evidence that these differences may not be as extreme as previously thought.” Funding for the Sloan Digital Sky Survey V has been provided by the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Heising-Simons Foundation, the National Science Foundation, and the Participating Institutions. SDSS acknowledges support and resources from the Center for High-Performance Computing at the University of Utah. SDSS telescopes are located at Apache Point Observatory, funded by the Astrophysical Research Consortium and operated by New Mexico State University, and at Las Campanas Observatory, operated by the Carnegie Institution for Science. The SDSS web site is www.sdss.org. SDSS is managed by the Astrophysical Research Consortium for the Participating Institutions of the SDSS Collaboration, including Caltech, the Carnegie Institution for Science, Chilean National Time Allocation Committee (CNTAC) ratified researchers, The Flatiron Institute, the Gotham Participation Group, Harvard University, Heidelberg University, The Johns Hopkins University, L’Ecole polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL), Leibniz-Institut für Astrophysik Potsdam (AIP), Max-Planck-Institut für Astronomie (MPIA Heidelberg), Max-Planck-Institut für Extraterrestrische Physik (MPE), Nanjing University, National Astronomical Observatories of China (NAOC), New Mexico State University, The Ohio State University, Pennsylvania State University, Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, Space Telescope Science Institute (STScI), the Stellar Astrophysics Participation Group, Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, University of Arizona, University of Colorado Boulder, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, University of Toronto, University of Utah, University of Virginia, Yale University, and Yunnan University. Coulter, age 79, of the Normantown Community, passed away on Saturday, August 8, 2026, in what she called “Memaw’s Cozy Cottage” in Wrightsville. She was born on September 26, 1946, in Jacksonville, Florida and lived there until moving to Georgia in 1968. She lived most of her life in Toombs and Tattnall Counties and earned an associate degree from Jacksonville University. She worked with Principle Health Care as a Data Quality Review Coordinator for twenty years. She was a member of Lyons Free Will Baptist Church. She always wanted everyone around her to be happy and did everything she could to bring joy to others. She enjoyed crafts, gardening, and spending time with family, but her greatest passion was her phone ministry and sending cards to people. She is preceded in death by her husband, James E. Coulter, Sr.; grandson, Jeremy B. Pittman; father, William B. Sturtervant; mother, Eva Liles Bauerle; and brother, Fred B. Sturtervant. Champion, the iconic American athletic and lifestyle brand, today announced a global partnership with V of BTS, introducing the internationally acclaimed artist as the face of its new True Champion campaign. Marking a new chapter for the brand, True Champion, celebrates the people shaping today's culture through their originality, perspective and enduring impact. Bringing together athletes, artists and creators from around the world, the campaign reflects Champion's commitment to those who inspire others simply by being themselves. Known for his unmistakable style, artistic vision and global reach, V embodies the spirit of True Champion. His influence extends beyond music, leaving an indelible mark across fashion, art and popular culture while connecting with millions of fans worldwide. "True Champion represents a new chapter for Champion and the values that continue to define our brand," said Stefani Fleurant, EVP, Marketing, Sport & Lifestyle at Authentic. "V's creative vision, global influence and genuine connection with his audience make him a natural partner for Champion. Together with an incredible cast of athletes, artists and creators, this campaign celebrates the many ways people inspire others through who they are and the incredible talent they bring to the world." Joining V in the FW26 campaign are Romeo Beckham, SOFI TUKKER, Kyle Kuzma, Danna Paola, Megan Keller, Bella Sims and Jaalen Best. Together, they represent a diverse group whose stories span sports, music and culture, reflecting Champion's global community and the evolving definition of what it means to be a champion today. The True Champion campaign will launch globally beginning August 10, 2026. Founded in 1919, Champion has been a pioneer in athletic and lifestyle apparel for over a century. Known for its iconic "C" logo and commitment to quality, innovation and selfexpression, Champion continues to inspire a new generation of consumers with collections that blend performance, heritage and modern style. Learn more at champion.com. Follow on Instagram and TikTok. V (Kim Taehyung) is a South Korean singer, songwriter and member of Pop Royalty BTS. Known for his captivating charm and distinct low pitch voice, V enriches the sound of BTS’ music. His solo discography includes “Stigma,” “Singularity” and “Inner Child.” He demonstrated his song-writing capabilities with “4 O’CLOCK,” “Scenery,” “Winter Bear,” “Blue & Grey,” and “Snow Flower.” He also participated in original soundtracks for Korean TV series, including “Even If I Die, It’s You” (‘Hwarang: The Poet Warrior Youth’ OST), “Sweet Night” (‘Itaewon Class’ OST) and “Christmas Tree” (‘Our Beloved Summer’ OST), broadening his musical scope. After starting off 2026 with handwritten letters to some of their most devoted fans, confirming their imminent comeback, the biggest band in the world dropped Arirang, their feverishly anticipated fifth studio album, in March, entering the Billboard charts at No. 1 and handily setting a record for the highest sales week for a group in over a decade. Soon after, the band members embarked on their blockbuster Arirang world tour, playing to sold-out stadiums all over the world. And just two weeks ago, they once again dominated headlines, announcing that they won’t submit music to next year’s Grammys, following the Recording Academy’s controversial announcement that it would include an Asian pop music performance category. But despite a busy year for OT7, the members—RM, Jin, Suga, J-Hope, Jimin, V, and Jung Kook—have also managed to pursue their own projects, flaunting the distinctiveness that has always endeared fans to the group. Today, V announces his global partnership with the iconic American sportswear brand Champion, in a campaign called “True Champion” that the company says highlights personalities shaping contemporary culture through their “originality, perspective and enduring impact.” The singer calls the brand “a natural fit,” with the values of the campaign personally resonating with him. “To me, being a ‘True Champion’ isn’t about trying to become someone special,” he says. “Just don’t try too hard to be someone else. I think the more you stay true to yourself, the more confident you’ll become.” V—who has been immersed in the fashion world through his presence at industry events and work with luxury brands—says partnering with Champion is perfectly in line with his life off duty. “I’ve always enjoyed mixing different styles instead of sticking to just one. High fashion is exciting, but I also appreciate clothes that feel effortless to wear,” he says. “When I’m at home, I’m usually dressed even more casually than people would think. I spend a lot of time in simple T-shirts and comfortable clothes because I like feeling relaxed. That’s probably why Champion has always felt familiar to me—it fits naturally into the way I actually dress when I’m off camera.” The campaign also hints at the singer’s passion for music and analog culture, featuring images of him playing the trumpet and standing beside a tower of cassettes. It’s an aspect of his personality that perhaps shone most clearly on his 2023 EP Layover, an intimate, low-key collection of jazz-inflected R&B. “There’s a certain warmth and nostalgia to analog culture, and I’m naturally drawn to that feeling,” he explains. “Vinyl is a good example. Even though Bluetooth speakers are convenient and sound great, I still prefer listening to vinyl records because the whole experience feels more personal and meaningful.” In a Vogue Japan interview from early this year, V talked about gravitating toward the color red. “I always try to include a hint of red [in my outfits],” he said. True enough, one of his Champion items follows that style rule: “My favorite is the gray long-sleeve shirt with the red Champion logo,” he says. “I really liked how the red stands out nicely against the gray and adds just the right pop of color. It’s casual, but the logo gives it just enough character.” Toward the end of the shows on the Arirang world tour, OT7 changes into casual clothes for the last section of the concert, highlighting the distinct personalities and the dynamic that have made the group so compelling. V’s own style has grown by leaps and bounds through the years. “Being in this industry, I’ve had the privilege of working with many different brands and seeing a wide range of styles over the years,” he says. “I’ve learned a lot from just looking at their collections and figuring out what works best for me, and that’s where I get much of my inspiration.” All of that sartorial experimentation has helped him land on a firmer sense of self. “My style is pretty instinctive,” he says. “I just go with whatever catches my eye and wear what feels right.
